detail:
The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) as a disorder that can develop after a person experiences or witnesses a traumatic event, such as a natural disaster, a serious accident, or an act of violence. Fear is part of the body's normal fight-or-flight response during and after trauma, and most people recover from their initial symptoms over time; NIMH notes that people whose symptoms continue may be diagnosed with PTSD. According to the National Center for PTSD, cited by NIMH, about 6 of every 100 people will experience PTSD at some point in their lifetime.

Symptoms usually begin within 3 months of the traumatic event, but they sometimes emerge later, and for a diagnosis they must last longer than 1 month and be severe enough to interfere with daily life, such as relationships or work. NIMH groups the symptoms an adult must have into re-experiencing symptoms, avoidance symptoms, arousal and reactivity symptoms, and cognition and mood symptoms; symptoms can include flashbacks, avoidance of reminders of the event, heightened reactivity, and negative changes in thoughts and mood. NIMH notes that a mental health professional with experience in PTSD can make the diagnosis, and that children and teens can react to trauma differently from adults.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms and diagnosis.
summary: NIMH describes PTSD as a disorder that can follow a traumatic event when symptoms continue beyond a month and interfere with daily life, affecting about 6 of every 100 people at some point in their lives.
takeaways: ptsd can develop after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event
symptoms must last longer than a month and interfere with daily life
about 6 of every 100 people experience ptsd in their lifetime
title: Post-traumatic stress disorder: when symptoms continue after a traumatic event
